doc.title: Howard Levy interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 11, 2025

title: Stories in the book: Tito Puente and a Chicago jobbing date
summary: He describes putting himself back into events, such as his first gig with Tito Puente and a jobbing date with a square bassist and AACM trumpeter.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Getting paid: wages, scale and the pay envelope

blocks.x: As you proceeded through the task of writing, did you find that you arrived at a place with adjectives and describing words that helped get the message across about the music you were doing? Because writing about music can be challenging and frustrating as well.

Yeah. You know it’s – the stories, it’s a far ranging range of stories. I mean music is in all of them, but some of them are more personal experiences with music as part of it. But of course I did you know, write out some changes, you know G seven sharp nine flat thirteenth and stuff like that. I wrote those kind of things out. I mean there was some very specifically musical things and I tried not to geek out too much on some of those things. But yeah it is hard. But I think what really made it work (I hope it works) is that I really put myself back into these events and started remembering how I felt while they were happening you know, like the first gig I played with Tito Puente and stuff like that. I mean you know these are very vivid memories in my head. And there’s another story of a jobbing date – do you call them casuals in New York?
Yeah, we call them club dates and casuals.

Club dates, that’s right, club dates. And in Chicago they’re called jobbing dates, where it was like this really square older guy who played like society two beat bass but hired all sorts of really, really good players, younger players, including a trumpet player who was in the AACM, to play a Christmas party for a bunch of phone company employees. And man, this guy just played so beautifully. It was unbelievable. I mean that’s why it’s in the book. I mean it was something that you would just never suspect happen. And every solo he took, the people stopped dancing and applauded like it was a concert. I mean this doesn’t happen, as you know. So that’s why there are certain stories in there that I just think are – hopefully it will show all these different sides of a musician’s life. You know, and the odd jobs that I had in the beginning before I was, you know, “don’t quit your day job” kind of thing, you know like before I was good enough to quit my day job, you
know. All sort of – the evolution of my musical life as it happened in all these different stages and steps.
